medium.conteudo_html:
Imagine You’re Running a Restaurant 🍳. Every day, you must:

  1. Receive fresh ingredients.
  2. Clean and prepare them.
  3. Cook the food.
  4. Serve it to customers.
  5. Check that everything went well.

Now imagine that you have 100 chefs, 50 recipes, and thousands of orders. You cannot simply shout instructions and hope everyone does the right thing!

You need a system that knows:

  • What needs to happen.
  • What must happen first.
  • Which tasks can run at the same time.
  • What to do when something fails.
  • How to monitor the entire process.

That’s exactly the problem Apache Airflow solves for data engineering. 🛠️

A data pipeline might need to extract data from an API, store it in cloud storage, transform it using Spark, load it into a data warehouse, and refresh a dashboard.

Each step may work perfectly on its own. But coordinating all those steps reliably is a different challenge.

That’s where Airflow comes in.

What Is Apache Airflow? 🌬️

Apache Airflow is an open-source platform for authoring, scheduling, and monitoring workflows programmatically using Python.

In simple words, Airflow coordinates tasks and makes sure they run according to your rules.

For example:

Airflow can schedule this workflow every day, enforce task dependencies, retry failed tasks, and show you what happened through its user interface.

But there’s an important distinction:

Airflow is an orchestrator, not a data processing engine.

It usually tells other systems what to do rather than processing enormous datasets itself.

Think of Airflow as the conductor of an orchestra. 🎼 Spark, dbt, databases, and APIs are the musicians. Airflow coordinates when they play, but it doesn’t play every instrument itself.

Why Do Data Engineers Need Airflow? 🤔

Let’s say you build a pipeline manually:

extract_data()
transform_data()
load_data()

This works for a simple script. But real production pipelines face many challenges.

  • Scheduling: How do you run the pipeline every day at 2 AM?
  • Dependencies: How do you prevent transformation from starting before extraction finishes?
  • Retries: What happens if an API temporarily fails?
  • Monitoring: How do you discover which task failed last night?
  • Backfills: How do you process historical dates after a failure?
  • Scalability: How do you coordinate hundreds of workflows?
  • Recovery: How do you rerun failed tasks without unnecessarily repeating successful work?

You could write your own Python scripts, cron jobs, logging, retry logic, and monitoring tools.

But you would gradually be building your own orchestration platform. 😅

Airflow provides many of these capabilities in one place.

It’s especially useful when your pipelines involve multiple systems, dependencies, schedules, and operational requirements.

The Most Important Airflow Concepts 🧱

Before writing code, let’s learn the building blocks. Once you understand these, the rest of Airflow becomes much easier.

1. DAG: The blueprint of your workflow

DAG stands for Directed Acyclic Graph.

Let’s break that down:

  • Directed: Tasks have a direction. One task leads to another.
  • Acyclic: The dependency path cannot loop back to an earlier task.
  • Graph: Tasks are connected like nodes in a network.

Imagine this workflow:

Notice that the sales and customer transformations can run in parallel after validation. The final loading task waits for both.

A DAG defines the workflow structure, schedule, and other execution settings. It doesn’t need to contain the actual heavy data processing logic.

2. Tasks: The individual jobs

A task is one unit of work inside a DAG.

Examples:

  • Download a CSV file.
  • Check whether a database table exists.
  • Run a SQL transformation.
  • Submit a Spark job.
  • Send a notification.

Each task has its own state, logs, retries, and execution history.

For example, if extraction succeeds but transformation fails, Airflow can show you exactly which step failed.

3. Operators: Ready-made task templates

An operator is a reusable template for performing a type of work.

Think of operators as tools in a toolbox. 🧰

Airflow also has provider packages that add integrations with cloud platforms, databases, Spark, and many other systems.

You don’t need to write every integration from scratch.

4. Task dependencies: Who goes first?

Suppose you have three tasks:

extract >> transform >> load

The >> operator defines the dependency direction.

It means:

  1. Extract must succeed before transform can run.
  2. Transform must succeed before load can run.

You can also define parallel work:

extract >> [transform_sales, transform_customers]

Both transformations can run after extraction succeeds.

To join them again:

[transform_sales, transform_customers] >> load

The final task normally waits for both upstream tasks to succeed.

5. DAG runs and task instances

These concepts sound similar, but they’re different.

  • DAG: The workflow blueprint.
  • DAG run: One execution of that workflow.
  • Task instance: One task’s execution within a particular DAG run.

Imagine a DAG scheduled every day.

On Monday, Airflow creates a DAG run for Monday’s data interval. On Tuesday, it creates another run for Tuesday’s interval.

The same task can therefore have many task instances across different dates and runs.

This distinction becomes important when debugging failures or reprocessing historical data.

Your First Airflow DAG: Let’s Write Some Code! 🐍

Theory is great, but let’s build something.

We’ll create a simple workflow that:

  1. Extracts sales data.
  2. Validates the data.
  3. Calculates total revenue.
  4. Prints the result.

The following example uses Airflow 3’s recommended airflow.sdk authoring interface. Older Airflow 2 installations may require different imports and scheduling conventions.

from datetime import datetime, timezone

from airflow.sdk import DAG, task

with DAG(
    dag_id="sales_pipeline",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
    schedule="@daily",
    catchup=False,
) as dag:

    @task
    def extract_sales():
        return [
            {"product": "Laptop", "price": 1000},
            {"product": "Phone", "price": 700},
            {"product": "Tablet", "price": 300},
        ]

    @task
    def validate_sales(sales):
        if not sales:
            raise ValueError("No sales data found!")

        for sale in sales:
            if sale["price"] < 0:
                raise ValueError("Negative price detected!")

        return sales

    @task
    def calculate_revenue(sales):
        revenue = sum(sale["price"] for sale in sales)
        print(f"Total revenue: ${revenue}")
        return revenue

    sales = extract_sales()
    validated_sales = validate_sales(sales)
    calculate_revenue(validated_sales)

What does this code do?

  • DAG(...) defines the workflow.
  • @task converts a Python function into an Airflow task.
  • schedule="@daily" schedules daily runs.
  • catchup=False prevents automatic creation of runs for all past intervals when the DAG is activated.
  • Calling one task with another task’s output defines a dependency.

Airflow automatically connects the three tasks because the validation task consumes the extraction task’s output, and the revenue task consumes the validated data.

Expected output

When the tasks run successfully, the revenue task logs:

Total revenue: $2000

The important part isn’t the calculation. It’s that Airflow now manages the workflow’s dependencies and execution history.

One warning: this example uses a small Python list for learning. Real production pipelines would generally read and write data through databases, object storage, or processing engines rather than keeping an entire dataset in memory or passing it between tasks.

Scheduling: How Does Airflow Know When to Run? ⏰

One of Airflow’s biggest advantages is scheduling.

Instead of running a script manually every day, you define when the workflow should run.

Here are common scheduling expressions:

For example:

with DAG(
    dag_id="hourly_pipeline",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
    schedule="@hourly",
    catchup=False,
):
    ...

This defines an hourly schedule. The ellipsis represents tasks you would add to the DAG.

A common mistake: confusing execution time with data time

Suppose your pipeline runs at 2 AM on October 10.

Which data should it process?

  • Data created during October 9?
  • Data created during October 10?
  • Data from the previous 60 minutes?

The answer depends on the schedule and how your tasks use the run’s data interval.

For scheduled workflows, Airflow commonly associates each run with a data interval. A daily run generally processes a defined daily interval, rather than simply meaning “process whatever exists right now.”

This matters enormously when handling late-arriving data, time zones, and historical reprocessing.

A good pipeline uses the intended interval to select its input data rather than blindly assuming that the current date is the date to process.

What is catchup?

Imagine you create a daily DAG today but set its start date six months ago.

With catchup enabled, Airflow may create runs for past scheduled intervals that have not yet been processed, subject to the DAG’s configuration and limits.

With catchup=False, Airflow does not automatically create that backlog of historical scheduled runs.

Use catchup when historical intervals genuinely need processing. Disable it when you only want normal forward-running schedules.

Don’t confuse catchup with backfilling: backfilling is the deliberate process of creating runs for historical intervals, with controls for how that work is executed.

How Airflow Works Behind the Scenes 🏗️

Now let’s look inside the machine.

A typical Airflow deployment has several important components. The exact architecture depends on the Airflow version and deployment method.

Let’s understand the main components.

1. The DAG processor

The DAG processor parses your Python DAG files and makes their workflow definitions available to Airflow.

If you write invalid Python or an unsupported import, your DAG may fail to load.

Practical lesson: a DAG that doesn’t appear in the UI may have a parsing error, not a scheduling problem.

2. The scheduler

The scheduler decides which task instances are eligible to run based on:

  • Dependencies.
  • Schedule and data intervals.
  • Previous task states.
  • Concurrency limits.
  • Other execution rules.

Think of it as the manager assigning work.

3. The executor

The executor coordinates how tasks are sent for execution.

Depending on the deployment, tasks may run locally, on separate workers, or through a distributed execution platform.

Common executor choices include:

  • LocalExecutor: Runs tasks through local processes.
  • CeleryExecutor: Distributes tasks to Celery workers.
  • KubernetesExecutor: Runs tasks in Kubernetes pods.
  • Other supported configurations: Depend on the Airflow version and deployment architecture.

The executor is not the same as the scheduler. The scheduler determines what is ready; the executor helps arrange execution.

4. Workers

Workers perform the actual task work in deployments that use separate worker processes or machines.

For example, a worker might execute a Python function that downloads a file or submit a Spark job to a cluster.

Not every deployment has a separate worker service. Some configurations execute tasks locally.

5. The metadata database

Airflow needs a database to remember what happened.

It stores information such as DAG runs, task states, scheduling information, and other metadata.

It is not intended to be the main warehouse for your business data.

Use your data warehouse, database, or object storage for the actual datasets.

6. The web interface

The UI lets you:

  • Inspect DAG graphs.
  • Check task states.
  • Read task logs.
  • Trigger DAGs manually.
  • Retry or clear task instances.
  • Review execution history.

This is one of Airflow’s biggest practical advantages: you can investigate a failed pipeline without guessing which Python script ran last.

Airflow’s official documentation explains these components and how they work together.

Retries: What Happens When a Task Fails? 🔄

Production pipelines fail. APIs go offline, databases become unavailable, networks time out, and cloud services experience temporary errors.

A reliable pipeline should not require a human to restart every temporary failure.

Let’s configure retries.

from datetime import timedelta

from airflow.sdk import DAG, task
from datetime import datetime, timezone

with DAG(
    dag_id="reliable_pipeline",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
    schedule="@daily",
    catchup=False,
) as dag:

    @task(
        retries=3,
        retry_delay=timedelta(minutes=5),
        execution_timeout=timedelta(minutes=20),
    )
    def extract_data():
        # Replace this with a real API or database request.
        print("Extracting data...")

    extract_data()

What happens here?

  • retries=3: Airflow can attempt the task again up to three times after its initial failure.
  • retry_delay: It waits five minutes between retry attempts.
  • execution_timeout: It limits how long an individual execution can run before timing out.

The timeout is useful when a task hangs indefinitely.

But here’s the important lesson! ⚠️

Retries do not magically make a pipeline safe.

Imagine a task inserts 1,000 records into a database and then crashes before reporting success.

Airflow may retry it. If the task inserts those same records again, you could end up with duplicates.

This is why experienced data engineers design tasks to be idempotent.
An idempotent operation can be repeated without producing unintended additional effects.

Useful techniques include:

  • Using unique keys and database upserts.
  • Replacing a specific date partition instead of appending it repeatedly.
  • Using transactional writes where appropriate.
  • Recording which batch or interval has already been processed.
  • Making external API requests safe to repeat when the API supports it.
My advice: always think about what happens if a task executes twice. That’s one of the most important habits in production data engineering.

This is just Part 1. In Part 2, we’ll explore Sensors, XCom, Branching and many more. Stay tuned! 🚀

medium.titulo: From Ticket to Verified Fix: Wiring Claude into Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions and Test Environments
medium.resumo: Most of a QA lead’s day is not testing. It is glue work: reading a ticket in Azure DevOps, finding the right branch on GitHub, kicking off…
medium.conteudo_html:
Most of a QA lead’s day is not testing. It is glue work: reading a ticket in Azure DevOps, finding the right branch on GitHub, kicking off a build, waiting for a deploy, checking that the test environment actually runs the new version, clicking through the repro steps, and writing it all back into the ticket.

None of these steps is hard. Together they eat hours, and every hand-off is a place where context gets lost.

Over the last months I wired Claude into that loop — Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions and our test environment — and turned our most repetitive QA routines into reusable playbooks. This article walks through the setup, four workflows we actually use, and the guardrails that keep it safe.

The setup: four connections and a folder of playbooks

The setup is less exotic than it sounds. Claude needs four connections:

  1. Azure DevOps through an MCP server — read work items, add comments, update state, create child tasks, query by WIQL.
  2. GitHub through the gh CLI — trigger workflows, watch runs, read PRs and commits.
  3. A browser pointed at the test or staging environment — log in with a test account, click through flows, take screenshots.
  4. The repositories themselves — so it can read code, test reports and history instead of guessing.

The real leverage comes from skills: short Markdown playbooks that describe one routine step by step — which repo, which workflow, what to verify, when to stop, what to write back to the ticket. Claude loads the right playbook when the request matches, so “deploy this branch to test” means the same sequence every time, no matter who asks.

Think of a skill as a runbook that executes itself, but still asks before anything irreversible.

Workflow 1: “Deploy this branch to test”

The most frequent request in a QA channel is some version of “can you put my branch on test?”. The playbook turns it into a predictable pipeline:

  1. Resolve the repo from an alias (backend, web, email, infra) and take the branch name exactly as given.
  2. Trigger the build workflow in GitHub Actions and wait for it.
  3. Trigger the deploy workflow only if the build succeeded. A failed, cancelled or timed-out build stops everything.
  4. Verify the runtime: call the backend’s version endpoint, or read the build version the frontend exposes, and compare it with the expected <release>-<run number> string.
  5. Report the build and deploy run links, the result of the check, and post a short comment on the work item.

Step 4 is the one humans skip. A green deploy job does not mean the environment runs your code — caches, failed restarts and parallel deploys all lie. Checking the version string takes seconds and kills a whole class of “works on my build” bug reports.

Workflow 2: Reproduce a bug straight from the ticket

Our bug template has fixed sections: Environment, Account, Preconditions, Steps to Reproduce, Expected, Actual, Evidence. That structure is what makes automation possible.

The playbook:

  1. Fetch the work item from Azure DevOps and parse the repro steps into those sections.
  2. Validate before acting. No login email? Vague step like “open some task”? No environment? Claude stops and asks one precise question instead of improvising.
  3. Set up preconditions — create the test data the steps need and record the IDs.
  4. Run the steps in the browser on test or stage, with a screenshot at each key point.
  5. Compare actual vs expected and write a reproduction report back to the ticket.

The same flow verifies fixes: run it once on the old build and once on the new one, and post a before/after comparison.

An unexpected side effect: ticket quality went up. When the first reader of a bug report is strict about missing accounts and vague steps, people start writing complete reports.

Workflow 3: The nightly E2E report — what broke, and why

Our Playwright + Cucumber suite runs every night and publishes a dashboard. Reading the diff between two runs is easy. Explaining it is the real work.

The playbook must answer two questions, in this order:

  1. What changed — scenarios that newly fail, scenarios that got fixed, grouped into clusters, plus what shipped in the app between the two runs (PRs, files, authors).
  2. Why it happened — each regression cluster must end in one of three verdicts, backed by evidence: a named app change, a data or environment event, or flakiness.

“We don’t know” is not an allowed ending.

The most valuable move is checking each failure against the actual release diff before anyone opens a bug. Often the honest answer is “this code didn’t change, the test is flaky” — and that saves a developer a morning of chasing a bug that does not exist.

Workflow 4: Grooming prep — QA joins before the code exists

Quality starts at the story, not at the test run. For stories tagged “Ready to Groom”, a playbook reads the story, its acceptance criteria and the parent epic, explores the frontend and backend code to see what already exists, and drafts a solution design as a child work item.

The team reviews and comments on that design. After the review, a second phase reads the discussion and creates frontend and backend tasks.

For QA this matters for one reason: testability questions — missing acceptance criteria, unclear permissions, edge cases — surface during grooming, when they are cheap to fix, instead of during regression, when they are not. The grooming meeting itself turns from a design session into a validation session.

Guardrails and lessons learned

Giving an AI access to your pipelines and tickets is only useful if people trust it. These rules earned that trust:

  • Test environments by default. Every playbook defaults to test. Anything else must be named explicitly.
  • Stop on red. No deploy from a failed build, no “let’s try anyway”. A failure ends the run and gets reported.
  • Verify, don’t assume. A green job is a claim; a version check on the running environment is evidence.
  • Ask instead of guessing. Missing account, vague step, ambiguous environment — one precise question beats a confident wrong run.
  • Test accounts only. Never real customer credentials; test data is created and recorded per run.
  • Write back to the ticket. Every run leaves a trace in Azure DevOps — links, results, screenshots — so the history lives where the team already looks.
  • Playbooks are code. Skills live in version control, get reviewed, and are improved when they fail — just like tests.

The biggest lesson: AI does not replace QA judgement. It removes the glue work around it, so the judgement gets more of your time.

What changed for the team, and how to start

The visible change is speed: a deploy-and-verify or a bug repro that used to need someone’s full attention now runs in the background and reports back. The less visible change matters more — every run follows the same steps, checks the same things and leaves the same trace in the ticket. Consistency is a quality attribute too.

If you want to try this in your team, start small:

  1. Pick the most boring routine your QA team repeats every week. For us it was deploy-to-test.
  2. Write it down as a playbook — repo, workflow names, what “done” looks like, when to stop.
  3. Connect only what that routine needs — usually your tracker and your CI.
  4. Run it side by side with a human for a week, then fix the playbook where it went wrong.
  5. Add the next routine.

The goal is not an AI that tests for you. It is a QA team that spends its time on risk, strategy and judgement — and lets the glue work run itself.

How does your team use AI around its pipelines? I’d love to compare notes in the comments.

medium.titulo: Nuxt 前端框架，還有 Server Middleware？從 HTTP 安全標頭開始和 nosniff
medium.resumo: 使用 Vue 開發時，我認為前端負責畫面，後端負責 API 和資料庫
medium.conteudo_html:
使用 Vue 開發時，我認為前端負責畫面，後端負責 API 和資料庫

最近在處理 Nuxt 網站的安全性設定時

Nuxt 明明是前端框架

卻可以透過 server/middleware 修改伺服器回傳的 HTTP Header？

原來 Nuxt 不只是 Vue 的前端開發工具，它也具備伺服器端的執行能力

Nuxt 不只是前端框架

在一般 Vue SPA（Single Page Application）中

伺服器主要提供 HTML、CSS 和 JavaScript 檔案

瀏覽器下載後，再由 JavaScript 產生畫面

Nuxt 則支援 SSR（Server-Side Rendering，伺服器端渲染）。

// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  ssr: true
})

當 SSR 啟用時

Nuxt 可以先在伺服器執行 Vue 程式、產生 HTML，再傳送給瀏覽器。

瀏覽器收到 HTML 後，會再透過 JavaScript 接手互動功能

這個過程稱為 Hydration。

因此 Nuxt 的程式可能在兩個不同環境執行：

  • Server（伺服器）：產生 HTML、處理 HTTP 請求。
  • Client（瀏覽器）：呈現畫面、處理使用者互動。

Nuxt 使用的伺服器引擎叫做 Nitro

它可以處理 SSR、Server API 和 Server Middleware。

Middleware 是什麼？

Middleware 中文稱為「中介軟體」。

可以把它想成辦公大樓的警衛。

當有人準備進入辦公室時，警衛會先檢查身分，確認符合條件才讓他進去。

Middleware 也是類似的概念

在主要處理流程之前，先執行某些工作。

Nuxt 有兩種容易搞混的 Middleware。

Route Middleware

放在：middleware/

主要處理頁面導航

例如檢查使用者是否登入。

export default defineNuxtRouteMiddleware((to) => {
  const isLoggedIn = false

  if (!isLoggedIn && to.path !== '/login') {
    return navigateTo('/login')
  }
})

Server Middleware

放在：server/middleware/

主要處理進入 Nitro 的 HTTP 請求

例如記錄請求資訊、設定 HTTP Response Header。

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  setResponseHeader(event, 'X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff')
})

兩者最大的差別是：

  • Route Middleware：處理使用者要前往哪個頁面。
  • Server Middleware：處理伺服器收到的 HTTP 請求。

為什麼需要 X-Content-Type-Options？

當瀏覽器向伺服器索取檔案時

伺服器會透過 Content-Type 告訴瀏覽器檔案類型。

Content-Type: text/html
Content-Type: application/javascript
Content-Type: text/css

但某些情況下，瀏覽器可能根據檔案內容自行猜測類型。

這種行為稱為 MIME Sniffing。

伺服器回傳：

Content-Type: text/plain

但檔案內容卻是：

alert("Hello!")

伺服器宣告這是普通文字，但內容看起來像 JavaScript。

如果瀏覽器在載入腳本時自行猜測類型並執行，就可能增加安全風險。

因此可以設定：

X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

要求瀏覽器在載入 JavaScript、CSS 等資源時，遵守對應的 MIME 類型檢查。

如果宣告的類型不符合要求，瀏覽器就會阻擋載入，而不是自行猜測後繼續使用。

使用 Server Middleware 設定安全標頭

在 Nuxt 專案建立：

server/middleware/security-headers.ts

import {
  defineEventHandler,
  setResponseHeader
} from 'h3'

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  setResponseHeader(
    event,
    'X-Content-Type-Options',
    'nosniff'
  )
})

這段程式其實只做一件事情：

在 Nuxt 伺服器處理 HTTP 請求時，替回應加入 X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff。

逐行來看：

  • defineEventHandler()：建立一個 HTTP 請求處理函式。
  • event：代表這次 HTTP 請求與回應的相關資訊。
  • setResponseHeader()：替 HTTP 回應設定 Header。
  • X-Content-Type-Options：安全標頭名稱。
  • nosniff：要求瀏覽器遵守對應資源的 MIME 類型限制。

因為檔案放在 server/middleware/，Nuxt 會自動註冊這段程式。

不需要在每個 Vue 頁面重複設定。

不過要注意，這個 Middleware 只能影響經過 Nitro 處理的 HTTP 回應。

如果正式環境還有 IIS、Nginx 或其他 Web Server 直接提供檔案，就需要另外確認。

如何驗證設定成功？

啟動 Nuxt 專案後，可以使用 Chrome 開發者工具確認。

  1. 按下 F12 開啟 DevTools。
  2. 選擇 Network。
  3. 重新整理網頁。
  4. 點選網頁的 Document 請求。
  5. 查看 Response Headers。
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html;charset=utf-8
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

這代表目前檢查的 HTTP 回應已經包含安全標頭。

另外，也應檢查 JavaScript 和 CSS 是否具有正確的 Content-Type

避免新增 nosniff 後造成檔案載入失敗。

重點整理

  • Nuxt 不只是前端工具，也具備透過 Nitro 執行伺服器端程式的能力。
  • SSR 可以在伺服器先產生 HTML，再交由瀏覽器接手互動。
  • Route Middleware 負責頁面導航與路由檢查。
  • Server Middleware 負責 Nuxt 伺服器端的 HTTP 請求處理。
  • Content-Type 告訴瀏覽器回應內容的類型。
  • MIME Sniffing 是瀏覽器根據內容自行判斷檔案類型的行為。
  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff 可以降低特定資源因 MIME 類型錯誤判斷而產生的安全風險。
  • 設定完成後，仍需要檢查 HTTP 回應，確認標頭確實生效。

medium.titulo: Why Do We Even Need React, Vue and Angular? 6 Things They Do So You Don’t Have To
medium.resumo: In the end, every one of them calls the same DOM methods you could call yourself.
medium.conteudo_html:
In the end, every one of them calls the same DOM methods you could call yourself. What they add is knowing when to call them, which ones to use, and which calls to skip.

Open the source of React, Vue or Angular and you won’t find any browser magic. They create elements with document.createElement, change text with nodeValue and textContent, and attach listeners with addEventListener, exactly like you would in a plain .js file.

So why does almost every team reach for one of them? It isn’t because the DOM is slow or because vanilla JavaScript can’t build a real app. These libraries make a long list of small decisions for you, on every click, and they get them right every time. You would get most of them right too, at least on the first day. By month six, with three teammates and forty screens, you’d be getting them wrong.

Here are the six that matter most. I checked each one against the shipped source of React 19.3, Vue 3.5 and Angular 21.2, and measured the browser side in Chrome 156. The interactive version of this post, with live demos you can run in your browser, is on allahabadi.dev.

1. You stop updating the screen by hand

This is the big one, and every other point in this post sits on top of it.

Take a small shopping cart. A cart icon shows a count, a list shows the items, a line shows the total, and the checkout button says how many items you’re buying. Four places on the screen show the same piece of data.

Without a library, every action has to remember every place:

<span id="badge">0</span>
<ul id="list"></ul>
<b id="total">0</b>
<button id="checkout">Checkout (0)</button>
const cart = [];
const badge = document.querySelector('#badge');
const list = document.querySelector('#list');
const total = document.querySelector('#total');
const checkout = document.querySelector('#checkout');
function addItem(item) {
  cart.push(item);
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.textContent = `${item.name} ₹${item.price}`;
  list.append(li);
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  checkout.textContent = `Checkout (${cart.length})`;
}
function removeLast() {
  cart.pop();
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  list.lastElementChild?.remove();
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  // checkout.textContent was never updated here
}

Nothing in that code crashes. removeLast just forgets the checkout button, so after you remove an item the button still says the old number. No error shows up in the console, and no test fails unless someone wrote one for that exact label. A real app has hundreds of these "update these four things" functions, and each new feature adds one more place each of them has to remember.

The fix is to flip the direction. Instead of writing “when this happens, change these elements”, you write one function that says what the screen should look like for any cart, and you call it after every change:

let cart = [];
function render() {
  badge.textContent = cart.length;
  list.replaceChildren(...cart.map((i) => {
    const li = document.createElement('li');
    li.textContent = `${i.name} ₹${i.price}`;
    return li;
  }));
  total.textContent = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  checkout.textContent = `Checkout (${cart.length})`;
}
function addItem(item) { cart = [...cart, item]; render(); }
function removeLast() { cart = cart.slice(0, -1); render(); }

(It uses the same four const elements as the first snippet.) Now no action can forget the button, because no action touches the screen at all. They change the data, and render draws the screen from it. People describe this as UI is a function of state: same state in, same screen out.

That is the whole idea React, Vue and Angular are built on. In React the same cart looks like this:

import { useState } from 'react';
export function Cart() {
  const [cart, setCart] = useState([]);
  const total = cart.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0);
  return (
    <>
      <span>{cart.length}</span>
      <ul>
        {cart.map((i, n) => <li key={n}>{i.name} ₹{i.price}</li>)}
      </ul>
      <b>{total}</b>
      <button onClick={() => setCart([...cart, { name: 'Tea', price: 40 }])}>Add tea</button>
      <button onClick={() => setCart(cart.slice(0, -1))}>Remove last</button>
      <button>Checkout ({cart.length})</button>
    </>
  );
}

But my vanilla render() has a cost the React version doesn't. It rebuilds the whole list on every click, even when only one item changed. Do that on a list of 2,000 rows and the browser throws away 2,000 elements and builds 2,000 new ones to change one price. Doing "render from state" without paying that price is the actual work these libraries do, and the next three sections are about how they do it.

2. They pick the right moment to touch the DOM

A browser tab runs your JavaScript and draws the page on the same thread. It can’t paint while your code is running. Roughly, one turn of the loop looks like this: run a task (your click handler), run the microtasks queued during it, run requestAnimationFrame callbacks, then recalculate styles, lay the page out and paint.

When you change the DOM directly, the change happens right there, in the middle of your handler. When you then read something that depends on layout (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect(), innerText), the browser has to stop and lay the page out right now, because the layout it has is out of date. Do that in a loop and you get one full layout per pass. This has a name: layout thrashing.

const rows = document.querySelectorAll('.row');
const heights = [];
for (const row of rows) {
  row.textContent = 'Read';        // write: layout is now out of date
  heights.push(row.offsetHeight);  // read: browser must lay out right now
}

The libraries never write to the DOM the moment you change state. They write it down and do all the DOM work later, in one go:

  • React collects every setState call made during an event. If your click handler calls setName, setCity and setAge, React renders once and commits once, after your handler returns and before the browser paints. Work that isn't urgent, like a startTransition update, goes through React's scheduler, which posts its work with MessageChannel and gives the main thread back every 5 ms so a keypress doesn't have to wait for a long render.
  • Vue puts each component that needs updating in a queue and flushes the whole queue in one microtask (Promise.resolve().then(flushJobs)). That is why you need await nextTick() to see the updated DOM right after changing state.
  • Angular in zoneless mode schedules change detection with whichever fires first, a setTimeout or a requestAnimationFrame, so a burst of changes in one handler leads to one check.

The core of the trick fits in six lines:

let queued = false;
function scheduleRender(render) {
  if (queued) return;
  queued = true;
  queueMicrotask(() => { queued = false; render(); });
}

Call scheduleRender(render) ten times in one click and render runs once.

One correction to something you’ll often read: none of the three uses requestIdleCallback to apply your updates. An idle callback can be delayed for a long time, and an update needs to be on screen in the next frame. Vue uses it for hydrateOnIdle, and Angular for @defer (on idle) blocks. Both are cases where waiting is fine.

You can do all of this by hand. You’d have to know that layout reads in a loop are expensive, that a microtask runs before the next paint, and that requestAnimationFrame exists. Then you'd have to make sure every developer on the team knows it as well, in every file.

3. They choose the fast DOM API for you

The DOM often gives you two ways to do the same thing, and one of them costs a lot more. The best-known pair is textContent and innerText.

textContent joins up the text nodes inside an element. It never looks at CSS. innerText returns the text as it appears on screen: it leaves out elements hidden with CSS, applies text-transform, and turns line boxes into line breaks. To know what is on screen, the browser needs up-to-date styles and layout. So reading innerText right after you changed something forces a full layout.

Writing is a different story, and this is where the usual advice gets it half wrong. In my traces, setting innerText did not force layout. It cost about the same as setting textContent. The only difference is that the innerText setter turns \n into <br> elements. The expensive part is reading it.

The read is easy to put in a hot loop without noticing, like this search filter:

const query = 'error';
for (const row of document.querySelectorAll('.row')) {
  row.hidden = !row.innerText.includes(query);
}

Setting row.hidden makes the layout out of date, and the next row's innerText needs it to be current, so the browser lays the page out again for every row. Swap innerText for textContent and that loop doesn't do any layout until the frame is painted.

Here is how React sets text on an element, from react-dom 19.3 (lightly reformatted):

function setTextContent(node, text) {
  if (text) {
    var firstChild = node.firstChild;
    if (firstChild && firstChild === node.lastChild && 3 === firstChild.nodeType) {
      firstChild.nodeValue = text;
      return;
    }
  }
  node.textContent = text;
}

If the element already holds exactly one text node, React changes that node’s nodeValue in place, which is the cheapest text write the DOM has. Otherwise it uses textContent. innerText doesn't appear anywhere in that path.

Most of the time, these libraries don’t read the DOM at all. The current cart, the current name and the current filter all live in JavaScript, in React’s fibers, Vue’s reactive objects or Angular’s views. When your code reads row.innerText to find out what a row says, it asks the browser to work it out from the page. A library already knows, because it rendered that row. Fewer reads means fewer chances to force layout, and you don't need to remember which layout-reading APIs are dangerous. I measured more than 40 of them in another post.

They skip updates that change nothing

Say a price on the screen is 499, and your code sets it to 499 again. Nothing on screen changes. Does the browser notice?

I tested it in Chrome 156 on a page with 3,000 paragraphs. Each test wrote the same value 200 times and read offsetWidth after each write, the way real code often measures right after updating:

  • el.textContent = '499' (same value): 200 layouts. textContent replaces the child text node with a brand new one every time, so the browser treats it as new content.
  • el.innerHTML = '499' (same value): 200 layouts, for the same reason, plus an HTML parse each time.
  • textNode.nodeValue = '499' (same value): 0 layouts. Chrome sees that nothing changed. A MutationObserver still received all 200 records, though.
  • el.style.width = '50px' (same value): 0 layouts. Chrome skips an identical inline style too.
  • if (el.textContent !== '499') el.textContent = '499': 0 layouts, 0 mutations.

So the browser skips some identical writes and redoes others, and the two most common ways of setting text are the ones it redoes. You’d have to know which is which.

const price = document.querySelector('#price');
for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
  price.textContent = '499';
  price.offsetWidth;
}

All three libraries put the check in front of the DOM, so they never need that list:

  • React compares old and new text before it marks a text node for update (current.memoizedProps !== newProps). One level up, if you call setCount(5) while the count is already 5, Object.is says nothing changed and React can skip rendering that component altogether.
  • Vue’s reactive setter runs hasChanged(value, oldValue) first. Assigning the same value to a ref doesn't trigger anything that depends on it.
  • Angular compares every template binding to its previous value with Object.is (bindingUpdated) and only touches the DOM when it differs.

All three compare with Object.is, so they check "is it the same value", not "does it look the same":

const user = { name: 'Asha' };
Object.is(user, user);              // true:  update skipped
Object.is(user, { name: 'Asha' });  // false: treated as a change

That is why in React you create a new object to trigger an update, and why a new object built on every render can cause updates you didn’t expect.

5. They treat text as text

This is the reason I’d add to the list. It saves teams from a whole class of security bugs without anyone thinking about it.

When you build UI by hand, the quick way to put a value into a page is innerHTML. It parses whatever string you give it as HTML. If that string came from a user, the user can write HTML into your page, including elements with event handlers that run their JavaScript under your domain. That attack is called cross-site scripting, or XSS.

const greeting = document.querySelector('#greeting');
const name = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('name') ?? '';
greeting.innerHTML = `Hi ${name}`;    // parses name as HTML
greeting.textContent = `Hi ${name}`;  // shows name as plain text

In React, <p>Hi {name}</p> always produces a text node, whatever name holds. Vue's {{ name }} and Angular's {{ name }} work the same way. To put raw HTML on the page you have to ask for it by name: React calls it dangerouslySetInnerHTML, Vue calls it v-html, and Angular runs anything bound to [innerHTML] through its sanitizer first. The safe way is the default, and the unsafe way is the one you have to go looking for.

6. They make a big codebase easier to work in

The first five points are things the library does at runtime. This one is about the people writing the code, and on a large team it may matter most of all.

  • Components. A <PriceTag> is written once, used in forty places, and changed in one file. With plain DOM code, "reuse" usually means copying a function and its HTML string into another file.
  • Clean-up has a home. Listeners you attach in the template (onClick, @click, (click)) are removed for you when the component goes away, and each library gives you one obvious place for the rest: the useEffect clean-up in React, onUnmounted in Vue, DestroyRef in Angular. By hand, every removeEventListener is yours to remember, and a forgotten one keeps the old element and everything it refers to in memory.
  • Tools that understand your app. React DevTools, Vue DevTools and Angular DevTools show your components and their current state, not just a tree of divs. Hot reload swaps an edited component while the page keeps running, often without losing what you typed into a form.
  • The editor catches mistakes. TypeScript checks JSX and Angular templates, so a misspelled prop or a wrong type shows up as you type, not as a blank screen.
  • A shared map. Routing, forms, data fetching and tests have well-known answers in each ecosystem. A new teammate who knows React already knows where state lives in your app and how a screen gets drawn. Hand-written DOM code is different in every company, and sometimes in every file.

When plain JavaScript is enough

None of this means every page needs a framework. This site is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework at all. A blog post, a landing page, or a form with a couple of toggles has very little state and only a few places that show it, so the bugs from the first section rarely have room to happen.

A simple rule of thumb: reach for a library when the same data shows up in several parts of the screen and changes often. That’s where updating by hand starts to break, and where batching, skipping and safe defaults pay for the JavaScript you ship. Below that point, a few addEventListener calls and textContent are perfectly fine.

React, Vue and Angular are still DOM code. They call the same APIs you can. The difference is that they pick the moment, pick the cheap method, skip the pointless call and escape the dangerous string on every update, including the ones nobody on your team thought about.

corrida_no_ar.resumo: A Maratona de Nova York quebra recorde mundial com mais de 61 mil concluintes, superando Londres. Conheça os melhores brasileiros na prova e veja a participação do prefeito como voluntário. Analisamos os números reais de corredores únicos na Maratona do Rio e uma polêmica nos…
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Terça-feira | 3 de novembro de 2026

A Maratona de Nova York de 2026 quebrou um recorde mundial histórico, tornando-se a primeira prova na história a ultrapassar a barreira dos 60 mil concluintes. A disputa pelo título de maior maratona do mundo estava acirrada: em 2025, Nova York registrou 59.226 finalistas, mas em abril de 2026, a Maratona de Londres superou essa marca com 59.830 corredores, comemorando o feito e até registrando no Guinness.

No entanto, a prova nova-iorquina deu o troco, atingindo a impressionante marca de 61.147 concluintes, um aumento de 3% em relação ao ano anterior. Além do recorde geral, a participação feminina também cresceu, saltando de 45,86% em 2025 para 47,73% em 2026, enquanto os homens representaram 52,41% dos participantes e os não-binários 0,26% (157 pessoas).

Com esses números, o ranking das maiores maratonas do mundo em 2026 ficou assim:
1. “Nova York:” 61.147
2. “Londres:” 59.830
3. “Paris:” 57.430
4. “Chicago:” 54.548
5. “Berlim:” 50.073

Prefeito de Nova York participa como voluntário

Um fato curioso marcou a Maratona de Nova York: o prefeito da cidade, Zelmon Mandane, foi visto trabalhando como voluntário durante a prova. Ele passou parte do dia distribuindo água para os corredores no percurso, um gesto que chamou a atenção e foi registrado por muitos participantes.

Os melhores brasileiros na Maratona de Nova York

Confira a lista dos cinco melhores corredores brasileiros, tanto no masculino quanto no feminino, que completaram a Maratona de Nova York em 2026:

“Masculino”
1. Jamal Soufane – 2:27:31
2. Leonardo Abaurre – 2:38:32
3. Dioni Souza – 2:43:01
4. Francisco Farias – 2:43:45
5. Josh Tolsdorf – 2:45:14

“Feminino”
1. Vitoria Gomes – 2:54:13
2. Carolina Susanna – 3:03:49
3. Janaina Santana – 3:04:15
4. Ana Carolina Guimarães – 3:05:44
5. Evelin Bombonatto – 3:05:59

Os números reais da Maratona do Rio

A Maratona do Rio divulgou seus números de 2026, e a análise revela um dado interessante. Embora o evento tenha registrado um total de 57.792 concluintes em todas as suas distâncias, o número de atletas únicos (pessoas diferentes) que participaram foi de 50.661.

A diferença se explica pelo “Desafio em Dobro”, em que um mesmo atleta corre mais de uma prova no fim de semana. Ao todo, 5.319 pessoas toparam o desafio, o que representa 10,50% do total de corredores únicos. A combinação mais popular foi o “Desafio Cidade Maravilhosa” (21 km + 42 km), com 1.658 participantes.

Nomes abreviados geram polêmica na Maratona de Aracaju

Os resultados oficiais da Maratona de Aracaju deste ano apresentaram uma particularidade: os nomes dos corredores foram exibidos de forma abreviada, mostrando apenas o primeiro nome e as iniciais dos sobrenomes. Essa prática, no entanto, fere a Norma 07 da Confederação Brasileira de Atletismo (CBAt), que regulamenta as corridas de rua.

O item 3.11.6 da norma é claro: “Os boletins dos Resultados Oficiais devem conter colocação, número de peito, nome completo, data de nascimento, faixa etária e as marcas de todos os participantes”. A abreviação dos nomes, provavelmente uma configuração do sistema de cronometragem da Cronomacx, impede a identificação completa dos atletas e pode gerar problemas para a organização junto à federação, além de dificultar a consulta de resultados por parte dos corredores.

Em resposta às críticas, a organização da prova publicou uma nota oficial em suas redes sociais, reconhecendo as falhas e pedindo desculpas aos atletas que tiveram sua experiência afetada. A organização se comprometeu a usar as sugestões para melhorar a edição de 2027 e afirmou que o compromisso da Speed Sports é sempre entregar o melhor evento, com responsabilidade e respeito.

Últimas etapas dos circuitos ASICS e Mountain Do

O circuito ASICS Run Challenge se prepara para sua última etapa do ano, que acontecerá em Florianópolis no próximo domingo, 8 de novembro. A prova oferece percursos de 4 km, 7 km e 15 km. As inscrições ainda estão abertas, e você pode usar o cupom `CORRIDANOAR10` para garantir 10% de desconto.

Já o Mountain Do anunciou seu calendário para 2027 com 10 etapas em 5 países, passando por locais como Colônia de Sacramento (Uruguai), Deserto da Namíbia, Ushuaia (Fim do Mundo), Fernando de Noronha e Deserto do Saara. O circuito é conhecido pelos kits caprichados, que incluem itens como uma mochila que se transforma em uma pequena necessaire. Utilize o cupom `CORRIDANOAR` para ter 10% de desconto nas inscrições.
